A group of about 30 Buddhist halls and monasteries cut into a horseshoe-shaped cliff above a river gorge in Maharashtra, western India. Their wall paintings, made between the 2nd century BCE and about 480 CE, are the finest surviving painting of ancient India.

The caves were made in two phases:

  • The early caves, from about the 2nd century BCE, date to the time of the Satavahanas. They include two prayer halls with a small stupa at the far end.
  • The later caves, the larger group, were cut in the 5th century CE. Many scholars date most of them to a short burst of about 460 to 480 CE under Harishena of the Vakataka dynasty, a contemporary of the Gupta Empire.

The paintings were made on a layer of plaster over the rock. They show stories of the Buddha's past lives, the Jataka tales, crowded with princes, dancers, animals, boats and palace life. The most famous figure, the Bodhisattva Padmapani in Cave 1, holds a lotus with a gentle downward look. Faces and hands carry emotion through pose and gesture, and the colours were made from local minerals.

After the 5th century the site was abandoned and the jungle grew over it. In 1819 a British officer, John Smith, came upon it while hunting a tiger and scratched his name on a wall. Copies and photographs then made Ajanta famous. Its style influenced Buddhist painting from Sri Lanka, at Sigiriya, to Central Asia. The Hindu, Buddhist and Jain caves of Ellora lie about 100 km away. Ajanta has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983.
